title: Domestication, Dispersal, and Human Selection
objective: Separate evidence about domestication history from the present native-range record and modern commercial origin stories.

terms.definition: Heritable change associated with repeated human cultivation and selection.
A locally adapted, historically cultivated population; the term requires provenance and should not be used as decoration.
Movement of genetic material between populations through crossing and backcrossing.
Loss of diversity when a population is founded or propagated from few individuals.

coreScience: Cannabis has been used for fiber, food, oil-rich achenes, ritual or intoxicating preparations, and medicine. Those uses created different selection pressures. Tall, less-branched plants can be useful for stem fiber; synchronized maturity and seed production matter in grain crops; flowering architecture and glandular trichomes became important in cannabinoid-rich crops.

Genomic studies have proposed an early domestication history in East Asia and divergence among ancestral, hemp, and drug-type groups. Kew’s present taxonomic distribution record lists a native range from Central Asia to Xinjiang and Pakistan. These statements answer different questions and should not be collapsed into a single simplistic “origin.” Human dispersal and selection were major contributors to present diversity, alongside natural population history, introgression, drift, feralization, incomplete sampling, and later breeding.

Modern cannabis is not a frozen survival of ancient regional types. During the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, breeders repeatedly crossed geographic and commercial lines, selected within small populations, propagated elite clones, and renamed material. A lineage claim should therefore be treated as a documented hypothesis unless supported by preserved pedigrees, accession records, or genomic evidence.
cultivationRelevance: Domestication explains why there is no single natural growth form or universal production target. Different selection histories influence flowering, architecture, fiber allocation, seed traits, and secondary chemistry.
Genetic conservation requires population-level thinking. Preserving one clone protects one genotype; it does not preserve the diversity of a seed population.

Domestication history becomes operationally useful when it is translated into traits rather than romantic origin stories. Record flowering response, branching, plant height, stem allocation, seed traits, chemical phenotype, stress response, and reproductive behavior directly. These measured traits are more useful for crop planning than assuming a regional label guarantees a production habit.

Conservation plans should preserve both identity and diversity. For a heterogeneous seed population, record how many individuals contributed seed, how parents were selected, whether relatives dominated reproduction, and whether seed was regenerated under conditions that could impose unintended selection. Repeated bottlenecks can change a population even when its name remains unchanged.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Record country or region claimed, the immediate breeder or institution, accession or seed-lot identifier, acquisition date, and the evidence supporting older geographic claims. Separate documented collection history from later commercial storytelling.

Record documented parents, filial or backcross generation, open-pollinated versus controlled mating, clone ancestry, and which pedigree links are verified versus reported. Preserve unknowns instead of filling gaps from reputation or phenotype.

Record number of seeds started, number of plants evaluated, number of males and females or mating parents retained, number contributing to the next generation, and any losses. These counts are needed to interpret bottleneck and drift risk.

Record the environment and management conditions under which selection occurred, the traits used to choose plants, measurement methods, selection intensity, and whether selection was intentional or resulted from survival, flowering time, disease, or propagation success.

Record seed storage conditions and regeneration date, clone or mother-plant identifiers, tissue-culture status, backup locations, and whether the method preserves a single genotype or a broader population. Link every preserved sample back to its source record.

Track flowering, architecture, fertility, chemistry, disease response, and other selected traits over generations. Unexpected shifts should trigger review of parent representation, contamination, labeling, drift, and environmental differences before a new origin claim is made.

misconceptions: Ancient means genetically unchanged: Cultivated populations evolve through selection, drift, crossing, and replacement.
A regional name proves landrace status: Provenance and population history are required.
One domestication paper closes the question: Conclusions depend on sampled populations, models, and archaeological interpretation.
evidenceLimits: Domestication and dispersal reconstructions depend on archaeological interpretation, present-day and historical sampling, demographic models, genomic reference quality, and assumptions about migration and introgression. Current taxonomic distribution, a genomic domestication hypothesis, a cultural history, and the provenance of a modern commercial line are different questions. No single paper or modern regional label should be treated as a complete account of cannabis origin or as proof that present material is an unchanged ancient population.
